title: ST558 Homework 2
text:
Task 1: Basic Vector practice
Suppose we have data from a medical experiment on blood pressure. We have the following pre-treatment values for subjects 1 through 20:
• 130, 128, 116, 124, 133, 134, 118, 126, 114, 127, 141, 138, 128, 140, 137, 131, 120, 128, 139, 135
after treatment, the subjects were measured again (subjects 1 through 20 match)
• 114, 98, 113, 99, 107, 116, 113, 111, 119, 117, 101, 119, 130, 122, 106, 106, 124, 102, 117, 113
1) Create two vectors. One vector corresponding to the pre measurements and one to the post measurements.
Solution:

# Pre-treatment blood pressure measurements
pre_bp <- c(
  130, 128, 116, 124, 133,
  134, 118, 126, 114, 127,
  141, 138, 128, 140, 137,
  131, 120, 128, 139, 135
)

# Post-treatment blood pressure measurements
post_bp <- c(
  114, 98, 113, 99, 107,
  116, 113, 111, 119, 117,
  101, 119, 130, 122, 106,
  106, 124, 102, 117, 113
)

pre_bp

 [1] 130 128 116 124 133 134 118 126 114 127 141 138 128 140 137 131 120 128 139
[20] 135

post_bp

 [1] 114  98 113  99 107 116 113 111 119 117 101 119 130 122 106 106 124 102 117
[20] 113


Above I created one vector for the pre-treatment measurements and another vector for the post-treatment measurements.
2) Assign names to the vector elements using the paste() function. Note that names() can be overwritten by a character vector. To quickly create the names, try running the code paste. Create the same names for each vector’s elements
Solution:

subject_names <- paste("Subject", 1:20, sep = "_")

names(pre_bp) <- subject_names
names(post_bp) <- subject_names

pre_bp

 Subject_1  Subject_2  Subject_3  Subject_4  Subject_5  Subject_6  Subject_7 
       130        128        116        124        133        134        118 
 Subject_8  Subject_9 Subject_10 Subject_11 Subject_12 Subject_13 Subject_14 
       126        114        127        141        138        128        140 
Subject_15 Subject_16 Subject_17 Subject_18 Subject_19 Subject_20 
       137        131        120        128        139        135 

post_bp

 Subject_1  Subject_2  Subject_3  Subject_4  Subject_5  Subject_6  Subject_7 
       114         98        113         99        107        116        113 
 Subject_8  Subject_9 Subject_10 Subject_11 Subject_12 Subject_13 Subject_14 
       111        119        117        101        119        130        122 
Subject_15 Subject_16 Subject_17 Subject_18 Subject_19 Subject_20 
       106        106        124        102        117        113 


3) Calculate the change in blood pressure for each patient by subtracting post-treatment measurements from pre-treatment measurements. Recall that R does math element-wise! Save this calculation as a new object (also a vector).
Solution:

# Calculate the change in blood pressure
change_bp <- pre_bp - post_bp

change_bp

 Subject_1  Subject_2  Subject_3  Subject_4  Subject_5  Subject_6  Subject_7 
        16         30          3         25         26         18          5 
 Subject_8  Subject_9 Subject_10 Subject_11 Subject_12 Subject_13 Subject_14 
        15         -5         10         40         19         -2         18 
Subject_15 Subject_16 Subject_17 Subject_18 Subject_19 Subject_20 
        31         25         -4         26         22         22 


A positive value means that the blood pressure decreased after treatment.
4) Calculate the average decrease in blood pressure across all patients.
Solution:
I used the mean() function to calculate the average change across all 20 subjects.

# Calculate the average change for all subjects
mean(change_bp)

[1] 17


From the result above we note that the average change is 17 mmHg.
5) Determine which patients experienced a decrease in blood pressure after treatment (a positive change). Use the which() function to just return the indices (and names) associated with this type of change.
Solution:
A positive change means that the pre-treatment blood pressure was greater than the post-treatment blood pressure. I used the which() to find the positions where the change is greater than zero.

# Find the subjects with a positive change
which(change_bp > 0)

 Subject_1  Subject_2  Subject_3  Subject_4  Subject_5  Subject_6  Subject_7 
         1          2          3          4          5          6          7 
 Subject_8 Subject_10 Subject_11 Subject_12 Subject_14 Subject_15 Subject_16 
         8         10         11         12         14         15         16 
Subject_18 Subject_19 Subject_20 
        18         19         20 


There are 17 subjects with a positive change. However Subjects 9, 13 and 17 are not in the list above since their blood pressure went up.
6) Subset the vector of differences to only return those that have a positive change.
Solution:
Now I subset the change_bp vector so that only positive changes are returned.

# Keeping only the positive changes
positive_changes <- change_bp[change_bp > 0]

positive_changes

 Subject_1  Subject_2  Subject_3  Subject_4  Subject_5  Subject_6  Subject_7 
        16         30          3         25         26         18          5 
 Subject_8 Subject_10 Subject_11 Subject_12 Subject_14 Subject_15 Subject_16 
        15         10         40         19         18         31         25 
Subject_18 Subject_19 Subject_20 
        26         22         22 


From above output we note that the subjects 9, 13 and 17 had increased blood pressure after treatment.
7) Calculate the average decrease in blood pressure for those where the blood pressure decreased (positive change).
Solution:

# Calculate the average decrease among subjects whose blood pressure decreased
mean(positive_changes)

[1] 20.64706


The average decrease among the subjects whose blood pressure decreased is 20.647.
Task 2: Basic Data Frame practice
1) Create a data frame object with four columns corresponding to your data above: patient, pre_bp, post_bp, and diff_bp
Solution:

#creating blood pressure dataframe
bp_df <- data.frame(
  patient = names(pre_bp),
  pre_bp=pre_bp,
  post_bp=post_bp,
  diff_bp=change_bp
)
bp_df

2) Return only rows where the diff_bp column is negative. (Use [ or learn about the subset() function if you’d like. If you use [, don’t reference the original vector from the first part, access the column of the data frame when looking at making a comparison.)
Solution:

#Return rows where blood pressure change is negavtive
bp_df[bp_df$diff_bp<0, ]

              patient pre_bp post_bp diff_bp
Subject_9   Subject_9    114     119      -5
Subject_13 Subject_13    128     130      -2
Subject_17 Subject_17    120     124      -4


These patients are the same numbers that had increased blood pressure after treatment .
3) Add a new column to the data frame corresponding to TRUE if the post_bp is less than 120. Recall you can use $ to reference a column. If you reference a column that doesn’t exist, and save a vector (of appropriate length in it), that vector becomes a column of your data frame! Similar to the previous question, don’t reference the original vector from the first part, access the column of the data frame when looking at making a comparison.
Solution:

#Add True or False based on post treatment blood pressure
bp_df$post_under_120 <- bp_df$post_bp <120
bp_df

              patient pre_bp post_bp diff_bp post_under_120

Subject_2   Subject_2    128      98      30           TRUE

Subject_19 Subject_19    139     117      22           TRUE

If post treatment blood pressure is under 120 then its True, else its False.

knitr::kable(bp_df)
